sentences.text: The dodo was an extinct flightless bird found only on the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean.
Subfossil evidence indicates the dodo stood between 62.6 and 75 cm tall and weighed between 10.6 and 17.5 kg.
The dodo had a robust skull with a hooked bill and a short cranium relative to its jaws.
Most historical representations depict the dodo with greyish or brownish plumage and a tuft of curly light feathers on its rear.
The traditional image of the dodo as a very fat and clumsy bird may be exaggerated.
A 1993 study by Bradley C. Livezey estimated male dodos weighed 21 kg and females 17 kg.
Based on weight estimates, it is suggested the male dodo could live to 21 and the female to 17 years.
Documents published in 2014 confirmed that a dodo sent to Nagasaki, Japan, in 1647 arrived alive.
In 2011, a box of dodo bones from the Edwardian era was rediscovered at the Grant Museum, University College London, where they had been stored with crocodile bones.
In June 2007, adventurers exploring a cave in Mauritius found, to date, the most complete and best-preserved dodo skeleton.
The dodo became extinct in 1662.
A dried head is the only remaining soft tissue specimen of the dodo.
The Dutch name "Walghvoghel" was first recorded in 1598 by Vice admiral Wybrand van Warwijck in his journal.
The Oxford dodo specimen was displayed at the museum from the 1860s until 1998 before being moved to storage.
The absence of competing mammalian herbivores on the Mascarene Islands allowed the dodo to evolve large size and flightlessness.
The dodo likely ate fallen fruits, nuts, seeds, bulbs, and roots.
The dodo used gizzard stones to digest a diet of fruits and lived in the woods of drier coastal areas of Mauritius.
Studies of the dodo's leg bone strength suggest it could run quite fast.
Researchers suggest the dodo's visual abilities reflect a shift to crepuscular activity to avoid heat and competition.
The dodo probably nested on the ground because it was flightless and had no mammalian predators on Mauritius.
The dodo was entirely fearless of humans because it evolved in isolation from significant predators.
Excavations suggest dodos became trapped in the Mare aux Songes swamp while trying to reach water during a severe drought approximately 4,200 years ago.
Fossils from the Mare aux Songes swamp show that dodos likely died trapped in the mud with their lower bodies preserved while their upper bodies were washed away or scavenged.
Although dodos were easy to catch, their powerful beaks posed a danger to hunters.

It is calculated that the raiding of nests by new species had a more devastating effect than hunting; specifically, pigs brought by humans to the island destroyed the dodo's eggs by raiding and eating them.
A 2023 study noted the dodo's loss negatively impacted native seed dispersal because introduced species handle seeds differently.
The dodo and the Rodrigues solitaire formed the subtribe Raphina within the pigeon and dove family Columbidae.
In 1842, Johannes Theodor Reinhardt proposed the dodo was a ground pigeon based on a skull found in the Natural History Museum of Denmark.
Genetic analysis placed the dodo within the pigeon family (Columbidae) alongside the Rodrigues solitaire.
The dodo likely lived in the woods of the drier coastal areas on the south and west coasts of Mauritius.
A 2003 statistical analysis by biologists David L. Roberts and Andrew R. Solow estimated the dodo's extinction date to be 1693, with a 95% confidence interval of 1688–1715.
The exact appearance and behavior of the dodo remain unresolved because historical portraits vary and few were drawn from live specimens.
During the 19th century, the Rodrigues solitaire and Réunion solitaire were sometimes classified as the same species as the dodo under different genus names.
Geneticists and conservationists plan to resurrect the extinct dodo and reintroduce it to Mauritius.
